data.title: eGain's (NASDAQ:EGAN) Conservative Accounting Might Explain Soft Earnings
data.description:
Shareholders appeared unconcerned with eGain Corporation's (NASDAQ:EGAN) lackluster earnings report last week. We did some digging, and we believe the earnings are stronger than they seem.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Zooming In On eGain's Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

Over the twelve months to September 2026, eGain recorded an accrual ratio of -0.37. Therefore, its statutory earnings were very significantly less than its free cashflow. To wit, it produced free cash flow of US$12m during the period, dwarfing its reported profit of US$7.61m. eGain did see its free cash flow drop year on year, which is less than ideal, like a Simpson's episode without Groundskeeper Willie.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On eGain's Profit Performance

As we discussed above, eGain's accrual ratio indicates strong conversion of profit to free cash flow, which is a positive for the company. Based on this observation, we consider it possible that eGain's statutory profit actually understates its earnings potential! Better yet, its EPS are growing strongly, which is nice to see. data.title: Is General Dynamics (GD) A Bargain Following Its New Navy Contract?
data.description:
General Dynamics (GD) is back in focus after securing a new US$194.1 million missile technology contract extension with the U.S. Navy, representing a fresh piece of work on a long-running program.

General Dynamics has seen the share price ease in the very short term, with a 1-day share price return that declined 0.49% and a 7-day move down 4.33%, even as fresh Navy work lands on its books. That softer near term tone sits against a steadier backdrop, with the 30-day share price return up 0.84% and the year to date share price return positive at 1.15%. Total shareholder return over 1, 3 and 5 years sits at 4.18%, 48.86% and 93.88% respectively, which points to long term holders still having been rewarded despite recent volatility and mixed headlines on insider selling, rare earth supply shifts and its large submarine and missile programs.

Scan how defense-focused contractors like General Dynamics stack up on quality and value using our hand-picked 35 high quality undervalued stocks.

General Dynamics now trades at a discount to both analyst targets and one intrinsic value estimate after this pullback. How far does that gap run before it starts to look stretched?

Most Popular Narrative: 6% Undervalued

General Dynamics last closed at $347.34, compared with a fair value of $370.92 implied by the most followed narrative. This leaves a modest gap that contract wins and execution risk will decide over time, according to CentryResearch, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who set out that view in the narrative.

The Navy never changed its mind, though. It kept paying GD in advance to buy parts and start early work, including $2.3 billion in May alone. You don’t buy parts for submarines you don’t plan to build. Then, on July 29, the Navy finally signed both deals: nine attack submarines and five missile submarines.

See why 22 investors see General Dynamics as 6% undervalued.

Across the whole narrative, CentryResearch leans heavily on contract visibility. A roughly decade-long submarine pipeline, a record backlog reported in the latest figures and a spread of work across aerospace, Marine Systems, Combat Systems and Technologies form the spine of the argument that the current discount is workable rather than extreme.

The analysis also stresses execution risk. Fixed price terms on the attack submarine deal, supply chain constraints that depend on third party yards and an incoming CEO with less shipbuilding experience all sit on the risk side of the ledger, alongside business jet cyclicality and potential shifts in future Navy priorities.

Set against those headwinds, the narrative highlights several supporting datapoints that matter for valuation work. Earnings growth of 7.4% a year over five years, a recent 10.5% profit increase that outpaced that longer run rate, net profit margins at 8.2% and a forecast earnings growth rate of 7.5% per year all feed into the $370.92 fair value estimate, which uses a discount rate of 8.20%.

On top of that, General Dynamics is assessed as having high quality earnings, a seasoned and largely independent board, a management team with an average tenure of 6.8 years and a reliable 1.83% dividend. Against those positives, readers should weigh the flagged significant insider selling over the past three months, slower forecast revenue growth than the wider US market at 4.5% per year and a forecast return on equity of 18.9% in three years that remains below a 20% threshold.

Analyst and model based checks outside the narrative also point in the same direction as the community view. At $347.34, the stock trades 17.2% below a consensus price target of $419.29 and 25.2% below one internal future cash flow estimate of $464.45. This suggests alignment between qualitative contract based arguments and quantitative fair value work, even if the methods differ.

For investors reading the narrative, the key question is less whether General Dynamics is undervalued in absolute terms and more how comfortable they are with the sources of that perceived discount. The gap to fair value in the story largely rests on the submarine backlog translating into sustained cash flows without eroding margins, while the rest of the portfolio, including Gulfstream jets and combat vehicles, continues to do its part.

Result: Fair Value of $370.92 (UNDERVALUED)

Still, fixed price submarine contracts and any prolonged supplier bottlenecks could compress margins and blunt the General Dynamics undervaluation story that investors are leaning on.

data.title: Intellicheck's (NASDAQ:IDN) Earnings May Just Be The Starting Point
data.description:
Even though Intellicheck, Inc. (NASDAQ:IDN ) posted strong earnings, investors appeared to be underwhelmed. We did some digging and actually think they are being unnecessarily pessimistic.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

A Closer Look At Intellicheck's Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Intellicheck has an accrual ratio of -0.21 for the year to September 2026. That implies it has very good cash conversion, and that its earnings in the last year actually significantly understate its free cash flow. In fact, it had free cash flow of US$5.6m in the last year, which was a lot more than its statutory profit of US$3.32m. Intellicheck's free cash flow improved over the last year, which is generally good to see.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On Intellicheck's Profit Performance

Happily for shareholders, Intellicheck produced plenty of free cash flow to back up its statutory profit numbers. Because of this, we think Intellicheck's underlying earnings potential is as good as, or possibly even better, than the statutory profit makes it seem! And on top of that, its earnings per share have grown at an extremely impressive rate over the last year. data.title: Textron Inc. (NYSE:TXT) Analysts Just Slashed Next Year's Estimates
data.description:
Today is shaping up negative for Textron Inc. (NYSE:TXT) shareholders, with the analysts delivering a substantial negative revision to next year's forecasts. Revenue and earnings per share (EPS) forecasts were both revised downwards, with the analysts seeing grey clouds on the horizon.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

After the downgrade, the consensus from Textron's twin analysts is for revenues of US$13b in 2027, which would reflect a not inconsiderable 15% decline in sales compared to the last year of performance. Statutory earnings per share are expected to be US$5.65, roughly flat on the last 12 months. Previously, the analysts had been modelling revenues of US$16b and earnings per share (EPS) of US$6.31 in 2027. Indeed, we can see that the analysts are a lot more bearish about Textron's prospects, administering a sizeable cut to revenue estimates and slashing their EPS estimates to boot.

Check out our latest analysis for Textron

Looking at the bigger picture now, one of the ways we can make sense of these forecasts is to see how they measure up against both past performance and industry growth estimates. These estimates imply that sales are expected to slow, with a forecast annualised revenue decline of 13% by the end of 2027. This indicates a significant reduction from annual growth of 4.3% over the last five years. By contrast, our data suggests that other companies (with analyst coverage) in the same industry are forecast to see their revenue grow 9.1% annually for the foreseeable future. It's pretty clear that Textron's revenues are expected to perform substantially worse than the wider industry.

The Bottom Line

The biggest issue in the new estimates is that analysts have reduced their earnings per share estimates, suggesting business headwinds lay ahead for Textron. Regrettably, they also downgraded their revenue estimates, and the latest forecasts imply the business will grow sales slower than the wider market. After a cut like that, investors could be forgiven for thinking analysts are a lot more bearish on Textron, and a few readers might choose to steer clear of the stock.
